title: Six students, one year of practice before asking (1.1)
hook: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
tomorrow: Q1: where do creatures come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday: consciousness is Brahman, prajnana, prajnanam brahma, the great saying that closed the Aitareya. Did you notice the knowing of something ordinary? Today, a new Upanishad, and six people with questions. Day four hundred five.

You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You've waited months. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year. Type the question, get the answer, scroll on. The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he says to them. Prashna means question. The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.
screen: `YOUR LIST OF QUESTIONS, READY.` → `COME BACK IN A YEAR.` → `PRASHNA MEANS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Tradition places the Prashna in the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha Bharadvaja. Satyakama Shaibya. Gargya Sauryayani. Kausalya Ashvalayana. Bhargava of Vidarbha. And Kabandhi Katyayana. The text says they were devoted to Brahman, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel in hand, sure he could tell them everything. Pippalada says: stay here one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like. And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers. He promises honesty. Think about what the year does. A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex. A question carried for a year, through practice, through ordinary days, has had time to become real. Some questions answer themselves. Some change shape. And the ones still standing are worth a teacher's time. Notice, too, the three things he asks for. Not cleverness. Not money. Discipline, a steady life, and trust. In the coming days, each student asks one question. The first five: where creatures come from, which powers hold up the body, where breath comes from, what's awake in sleep, and what happens to the one who meditates on om.
screen: `SIX STUDENTS, FUEL IN HAND.` · `STAY ONE MORE YEAR.` · `IF WE KNOW, WE'LL TELL YOU.` · `A QUESTION CARRIED BECOMES REAL.` · then, large: `EARN THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of waiting, the way Pippalada's students waited. Sit, and let the body settle. When the urge comes to move, check something, or get on with the day, notice it and stay. That's a small tapas. Keep it simple: one breath, then the next. And trust the bell to keep the time, so you don't have to. If a question rises, let it stand at the door, fuel in hand, until later. The bell holds the time.
Six students. The seekers of the Prashna Upanishad, told by the sage Pippalada to live a year in discipline and faith before asking, and promised only: if we know, we'll tell you.
Your line: earn the question. Today, before you search for the answer to something, carry the question a little longer, and see if it changes. Day four hundred five.

screen: `DAY 405 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?`

howItsDone: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; some Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

original.note: Sanskrit praśna, question: the Prashna Upanishad is built from six students' six questions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good teacher answers right away.
what it means: Pippalada asks his students to practice for a year first, and promises only honesty.
what a scholar hears: yadi vijñāsyāmaḥ, sarvaṃ ha vo vakṣyāma iti, 'if we know, we shall tell you all' (Prashna 1.2). the Upanishad belongs to the Atharva Veda.

Editor review (2026-10-01): six students ask six questions, so 'over the next five days, each student will ask one' miscounted; names now given as the text gives them (Sukesha Bharadvaja, Satyakama Shaibya, Gargya Sauryayani, Kausalya Ashvalayana, Bhargava Vaidarbhi, Kabandhi Katyayana) instead of guessed parentage ('grandson of Surya'); the practice repeated day 396's hold-a-question practice and now enacts the year's discipline, simplicity and trust; cut 'we live in a world of instant answers'.
